name: Old Swiss Confederacy
summary: A league of Alpine cantons that defended its freedom against the Habsburgs from 1291, became famous for its pikemen and mercenaries, and was ended by the French invasion of 1798.

location.value: The page gives no area in km². The confederacy grew by purchase and conquest, adding Aargau in 1415, Thurgau in 1460 and Ticino by 1515.

terrain.value: The high Alps in the south, the Jura hills in the north-west, and the lower Swiss plateau with its lakes between them.

climate.value: Cold alpine climate in the mountains and a cooler temperate climate on the plateau; the Little Ice Age brought colder summers after about 1550.

resources.value: Alpine pastures for cattle, cheese and butter, timber, water power, and control of trade routes over passes such as the Gotthard.

disasters.value: Avalanches, rockfalls and floods in the Alps; the Basel earthquake of 1356, the strongest known in central Europe, destroyed much of the city.

population.value: Not stated on the page. The entry’s 1.7 million in 1798 is unconfirmed.

urbanisation.value: Mostly villages; the main cities were Zürich, Bern, Basel and Lucerne, each with perhaps 5,000–10,000 people around 1500, plus allied Geneva.

disease.value: Repeated plague outbreaks from the Black Death (1348–49) until the late 1600s, with heavy deaths in cities such as Basel and Zürich.

migration.value: Many young men served abroad as mercenaries.

economicBase.value: Many Swiss served privately as mercenaries in the Italian Wars.

tradeRoutes.value: The Gotthard Pass, opened to traffic around 1230, linked Germany with Milan; Basel and Geneva were trade hubs on the Rhine and Rhône.

wealth.value: Modest overall, but city patricians and mercenary captains grew rich from trade, pensions paid by foreign kings, and later textiles.

moneyAndTax.value: No common currency: each canton and city minted its own coins (such as the Bernese batzen); taxes were light and set locally.

inequality.value: Ruling cantons governed subject lands such as Aargau, Thurgau and Ticino, and city patricians ruled rural peasants, leading to the Peasants’ War of 1653.

governmentType.value: A loose confederation of independent small states that grew from eight to thirteen cantons by the early 1500s, with allied associates and jointly ruled territories alongside the full members.

keyRulers.value: No single ruler: a loose confederation of independent small states whose diet was the Tagsatzung. Zwingli is not named on the page, which says only that the Reformation split the cantons into Protestant and Catholic camps (the Wars of Kappel).

succession.value: No monarch: cantons were run by councils in the cities and by open-air assemblies (Landsgemeinde) in rural cantons such as Uri and Schwyz.

institutions.value: The Diet (Tagsatzung), a meeting of envoys from the cantons that decided shared matters, plus agreements such as the Stanser Verkommnis (1481).

stability.value: The Reformation divided the cantons into Protestant and Catholic; Wars of Kappel in 1529 and 1531.

eliteConflict.value: After the Reformation, Catholic central cantons opposed Protestant cities such as Zürich and Bern; city and rural cantons also clashed.

armyAndTech.value: Infantry with long pikes and halberds in disciplined squares that beat armoured knights; Swiss mercenaries served France and the Pope (Swiss Guard, 1506).

majorWars.value: Victories over the Habsburgs in 1315 (battle not named), at Sempach in 1386 and at Näfels in 1388; the “Burgundy Wars of the 1470s” (no exact years); the confederacy fell to a French invasion in 1798.

territoryChange.value: Grew from 3 founding cantons (Uri, Schwyz, Unterwalden) in 1291 to 13 cantons by 1513, plus allied and subject lands.

alliancesRivals.value: Fought the Habsburgs (Morgarten 1315, Sempach 1386), Burgundy (1474–77) and the emperor in the Swabian War (1499); allied with France from 1516.

inventions.value: Few inventions, but Swiss scholars such as Paracelsus, the Bernoulli family and Leonhard Euler of Basel made major advances in medicine and mathematics.

scienceEducation.value: The University of Basel (1460) was the only university; Erasmus, Paracelsus, the Bernoullis and Euler all worked in Basel.

openness.value: Neutral in European wars after defeat at Marignano (1515), yet open to trade, foreign military service and Protestant refugees such as the Huguenots.

communicationTransport.value: Mule tracks over Alpine passes such as the Gotthard and Great St Bernard, and boats on the lakes and on the Rhine and Aare rivers.

religion.value: The Reformation led to doctrinal division among the cantons; the page does not name Zwingli.

languageWriting.value: Mostly Swiss German dialects, with French in western lands such as Vaud and Italian in Ticino; German was used for official records.

artsArchitecture.value: Arcaded old towns such as Bern, painted Renaissance houses, Lucerne’s Chapel Bridge (1333), and painters Hans Holbein the Younger and Urs Graf in Basel.

socialStructure.value: Free peasants and herders in rural cantons, guild burghers and patrician families in the cities, and subject peasants in conquered lands.

sharedIdentity.value: A loose sense of Swiss unity built on oaths of alliance, the legends of the Rütli oath and William Tell, and shared wars against the Habsburgs.

dailyLife.value: Most families farmed or herded cattle, moving herds to high summer pastures and making cheese; townspeople worked in crafts governed by guilds.

neighbours.value: Holy Roman Empire, France, Milan, Savoy.

ideasReligions.value: The Reformation led by Huldrych Zwingli in Zürich (from 1519) and John Calvin in Geneva (from 1541) spread Reformed Protestantism across Europe.

colonisation.value: No overseas colonies, but the cantons conquered and ruled subject lands such as Aargau (1415), Thurgau (1460), Vaud (1536) and Ticino.

riseSignals.value: The Federal Charter of 1291 among Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden, regarded since 1889 as the founding document.

peakPeriod.value: Expanded to eight cantons, then ten in 1481, twelve in 1501 and thirteen by 1513.

declineSignals.value: Defeat at Marignano (1515) led to neutrality.

outcome.value: Recognised as independent of the Holy Roman Empire in 1648; fell to a French invasion in 1798 and became the Helvetic Republic.

overallCertainty.value: Basic facts are well documented; some figures are estimates.
